title: Power over Ethernet: The Complete Beginner's Guide

scenes.narration: One cable. Data and power together. No wall socket needed. That's power over Ethernet.

scenes.heading: The power strip
scenes.narration: A TV, a console and a soundbar each need a signal and a socket. A power strip lets one wall outlet feed several devices, but it has a total wattage limit. Go over it, and the breaker trips. Think of your switch as that power strip. Each port is a socket, and the switch's power supply is the wall outlet. The P o E standards say how much power each socket can give. And the switch has a total budget to share.

scenes.heading: Power levels
scenes.narration: There are three standards to know. A F gives fifteen point four watts per port. A T, called P o E plus, gives thirty. And B T goes up to sixty, or even a hundred watts.

scenes.heading: Checking your power
scenes.narration: To check power, use show power inline. By default, ports are on auto, which negotiates just what's needed. Static reserves the full amount. And never turns power off.

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three mix-ups. Not every P o E switch gives thirty watts. Check the standard. A normal device with an Ethernet port won't get power. It needs to be a powered device. And static mode wastes budget, because it reserves the maximum.

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.narration: So, to recap. P o E sends power and data over one cable. Learn the three levels: fifteen, thirty and up to a hundred watts. And remember the switch has a total power budget. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva PoE lab.
